Why this one matters

Two final places, decided in one afternoon

The Nations Championship splits twelve teams into northern and southern tables. Only the top side in each table reaches the Grand Final at Twickenham on Sunday 29 November (16:40) — everyone else plays a placing match on Finals Weekend. After five rounds, five teams can still make it, and this match touches both races at once.

A win is worth 4 points, plus a bonus point for four tries and another for losing by seven or fewer. Level teams are split on wins, then points difference. Tables after Round 5, Sunday 15 November.

ENG

What England need

  • Finish above France and Ireland. England start one point behind France (21) and level with Ireland (20), but with by far the best points difference (+134).
  • Take one more point than France on the day — and at least as many as Ireland — and England top the north. A tie on points almost certainly favours England on points difference.
  • A bonus-point win settles it unless France also win with a bonus point against Argentina (20:10, Paris) — France kick off last and will know exactly what they need.
  • Ireland host South Africa at 16:40, after this match ends — England's result sets their target.
NZL

What the All Blacks need

  • Match South Africa's return. New Zealand lead the south by one point (22 to 21): take at least as many points at Twickenham as the Springboks take in Dublin and they top the table.
  • A bonus-point win guarantees the final, whatever happens in Ireland v South Africa.
  • A tie on points goes to South Africa — the Boks' points difference (+138) is 72 better, so the All Blacks cannot afford to finish level.
  • This game finishes before Ireland v South Africa kicks off, so the pressure lands squarely on Rassie Erasmus's side afterwards.

Form guide

Arriving from opposite directions

England put 78 points and 13 tries on Japan last Saturday — winger Will Joseph scored five on his first Test start. On the same afternoon in Cardiff, Wales beat the All Blacks 35–28, their first win over New Zealand since 1953, ending 34 straight defeats. The All Blacks still left with two bonus points (four tries, losing by seven) — which is why they still lead their table.

Who's fit, who's out — as at Wednesday 18 November

ENG

England — Borthwick

  • Back in contention: Ollie Chessum, George Furbank and Seb Atkinson all return to the 36-man training squad at Pennyhill Park after injury.
  • Out: Immanuel Feyi-Waboso (ankle) misses the autumn.
  • Selection headache: Will Joseph's five tries against Japan give Borthwick a genuine call to make out wide.
  • Fly-half options: George Ford, Fin Smith and Marcus Smith are all in the squad.
  • Key forwards: captain Maro Itoje, Ellis Genge, Jamie George, Ben Earl and Henry Pollock headline a settled pack.

Full 36: Baxter, Chessum, Clark, Coles, Cowan-Dickie, B. Curry, Dan, Earl, Fisilau, George, Genge, Heyes, Itoje, Iyogun, Kenningham, Martin, Opoku-Fordjour, Pearson, Pollock, Stuart; Atkinson, Dingwall, Ford, Freeman, Furbank, Joseph, Marchant, McParland, Ojomoh, Slade, F. Smith, M. Smith, Spencer, Steward, Van Poortvliet.

NZL

New Zealand — Rennie

  • Out for the tournament: lock Jamie Hannah (fractured shoulder blade) and centre Quinn Tupaea (fractured thumb, needs surgery) — both hurt in Cardiff and flying home.
  • Called up: Sam Darry (lock) and Billy Proctor (midfield) join the squad in London.
  • Expected back: Jordie Barrett (head injury), plus Cam Roigard, Damian McKenzie, captain Codie Taylor and Fabian Holland, all rested against Wales.
  • A chance: Will Jordan ran at about 80% on his hamstring on Monday with no issues — Rennie rates him a chance for Saturday.
  • Midfield reshuffle: Anton Lienert-Brown is the likely replacement at centre alongside Jordie Barrett.

Rennie has promised his strongest side and admitted his team “let the country down” in Cardiff. The squad are even considering loudspeakers at training to prepare for the Twickenham noise.

The rivalry

121 years, and England still chase

Head-to-head — all Tests

PlayedNZ winsEng winsDraws
47 since 19053692

First meeting: 2 December 1905, Crystal Palace — the touring “Originals” won 15–0, Duncan McGregor scoring four tries. England's first win came in 1936 (13–0, Prince Alexander Obolensky scoring twice). Since 2008 the sides have contested the Hillary Shield, named for Sir Edmund Hillary.

England hold the Shield after last year's 33–19 win. Beat them again on Saturday and it would be only the second time England have ever beaten the All Blacks in consecutive Tests — the first was in 2002–03.

Last five meetings

England 33–19 New Zealand Eng15 Nov 2025 · Twickenham
England 22–24 New Zealand NZ2 Nov 2024 · Twickenham
New Zealand 24–17 England NZ13 Jul 2024 · Auckland
New Zealand 16–15 England NZ6 Jul 2024 · Dunedin
England 25–25 New Zealand Draw19 Nov 2022 · Twickenham

Four of the last five were decided by seven points or fewer. The exception is the one England remember: 2025's win was their first over the All Blacks at Twickenham since 2012 — recovering from 12–0 down with 25 unanswered points.
